correctness.rationale: The known maximum length is \(n-2\) for every \(n\ge4\). The first selected vertex footprints exactly three vertices, so every later term in a maximum sequence must footprint exactly one. While at least two consecutive vertices remain undominated, exactly the two dominated frontier vertices can do this; when one remains, exactly three terminal choices can. This gives a bijective \(n\cdot2^{n-4}\cdot3\) encoding and the omitted-pair classification. Splitting terminal choices and using dihedral transitivity gives the per-set multiplicities. Exhaustive replay for \(3\le n\le10\) independently checks the boundary cases and counts.

value.rationale: Cycles are a canonical family for Grundy domination, but the standard literature records the maximum length rather than the extremizers. The theorem answers the natural next extremal question completely: it separates ordered sequences from underlying maximum sets, identifies the exact support geometry, and exposes exponentially different ordering multiplicities for the two support types. This is a structural classification, not a routine recomputation of the scalar invariant.
